summary: An RTCP Canonical Name is a persistent identifier for an RTP endpoint, staying the same even when its SSRC changes. This standards-track document gives guidelines for choosing CNAMEs so that they are unique and keep working. It was replaced by RFC 7022.

eli5.summary: On a video call, your temporary number might change, but your name tag stays. This advises how to make name tags that don't clash. It was later replaced by RFC 7022.

questions: how to choose rtp canonical name
subtitle: Better ways to pick persistent identifiers for endpoints in RTP sessions.

tldr.problem: RTP endpoints need persistent identifiers (RTCP CNAMEs) that stay constant even when temporary session identifiers change, but old guidelines using domain names or IP addresses produce duplicates.
tldr.mechanism: This document specifies methods to generate unique, persistent CNAMEs using UUIDs for long-term use or MAC addresses and cryptographic hashing for per-session identifiers.
tldr.outcome: OSPFv3 implementations can now authenticate packets without depending on IPsec, which is difficult to configure in some environments like mobile networks. This RFC was replaced by RFC 7022.

today: RFC 6222 is now Historic, as it was replaced by RFC 7022, which provides updated guidelines for RTCP CNAME selection.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) uses a Canonical Name (CNAME) as a persistent identifier for an endpoint, separate from the temporary Synchronization Source (SSRC) identifier that may change if a collision is detected or the application restarts. While the RFC 3550 standard for RTP provided guidance on choosing a CNAME, in practice those methods often fail to guarantee uniqueness within a session.

This document updates RFC 3550 with new guidelines that allow endpoints to choose unique RTCPCNAMEs reliably. The primary goal is to ensure that every endpoint in an RTP session has a different CNAME, enabling tracking of media streams and synchronization of related streams even as session identifiers change.
sections.eli5: Each person on a video call needs a unique name tag that stays the same. The old rules for picking names sometimes let two people get the same one. This document gives better rules.

sections.title: Problems with Old Methods
sections.content:
RFC 3550 recommended using fully qualified domain names (FQDNs) as the host part of a CNAME. However, in large service provider networks, FQDNs are no longer necessarily unique: many endpoints may share the same domain name.

The standard also suggested using IPv4 addresses. This approach breaks down when multiple hosts share the same address through Network Address Translation (NAT) or when they use private network addresses. Additionally, endpoints behind translators that convert from private to public addresses may end up with non-unique CNAMEs if not carefully configured.

These practical limitations mean the old guidelines cannot guarantee uniqueness without relying on manual configuration, which does not scale well.
sections.eli5: The old way said to use your domain name or IP address as your name tag. But many people might have the same domain name, and multiple machines might share one IP address (especially through NAT). So those methods don't work.

sections.title: Choosing Unique CNAMEs
sections.content:
The document defines two types of CNAMEs. A persistent CNAME stays the same across multiple RTP sessions and is essential when an endpoint needs to synchronize multiple related media streams, such as audio and video in a multimedia session. A per-session CNAME is generated fresh for each session, which limits tracking by third parties and provides some privacy protection.

For persistent CNAMEs, endpoints MUST generate and store a UUID (Universally Unique Identifier) as specified in RFC 4122, in version 1, 2, or 4 form, producing a 36-character string. Alternatively, for short-term persistence, endpoints MAY use the least significant 48 bits of a Media Access Control (MAC) address from the interface that initiates the session, formatted in colon-separated hexadecimal notation (e.g., "00:23:32:af:9b:aa").

For per-session CNAMEs, a new identifier is generated for each session following a procedure that combines current time, system-specific identifiers, and session details, hashed using SHA-256 and encoded in Base64 to produce a 16-character string.
sections.eli5: You can pick your name tag one of two ways. For a long-term tag, generate and save a unique UUID or use your network card's permanent address. For a one-time tag, mix together the current time and session details, hash them, and use the result. Both methods ensure no one else picks the same tag.

sections.title: Generating a Unique Identifier
sections.content:
When endpoints need to generate a unique identifier (such as for per-session CNAMEs or MAC-address-based persistent ones), they follow a cryptographic procedure. First, obtain the current time in 64-bit NTP format. Second, obtain a modified EUI-64 identifier from the system, or derive one from a 48-bit MAC address, or use a system-specific identifier like a serial number if neither is available.

Third, concatenate the time with the system-specific identifier to form a key. If generating a per-session CNAME, also concatenate the RTP endpoint's initial SSRC and the source and destination IP addresses and ports. Finally, compute the SHA-256 cryptographic hash of the key.

This procedure ensures that even endpoints on the same host or network can generate identifiers that are unique with very high probability, because the combination of time, system identity, and (for per-session CNAMEs) session details makes collisions astronomically unlikely.
sections.eli5: To generate your name tag, take the current time and your machine's unique identifier, mix them together, and hash them with SHA-256. The result is a number that almost certainly no one else will ever pick.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document emphasizes that these methods ensure uniqueness with very high probability, but implementations MUST NOT rely on CNAME uniqueness for essential security services. Participants in an RTP session are trusted not to impersonate each other: because each participant freely chooses their own CNAME, a malicious endpoint can deliberately select someone else's CNAME.

The hash function used (SHA-256) is employed for its randomness properties, but no cryptographic security assumptions are made about it. The procedure is not assumed to be collision-resistant against an attacker, because an attacker attempting impersonation would simply set the CNAME directly rather than trying to break the hash function.

The input data to the CNAME generation algorithm (time, system identifiers, session details) is not kept confidential. A third party observing a CNAME might be able to determine its inputs and thus correlate RTP sessions from the same endpoint. Applications concerned about this can generate per-session CNAMEs instead, which do not carry identifying information across sessions.
sections.eli5: These methods are very good at preventing accidental name clashes, but a bad actor could still lie and pick someone else's name. The encryption is just to make sure random name collisions do not happen, not to provide security against attack. If you want to stay anonymous, use a new name tag for each call.
